Country, northeastern Africa and southwestern Asia (via the [[Sinai Peninsula]]), officially the Arab Republic of Egypt. It is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the north, Palestine and Israel to the northeast, the Red Sea to the east, Sudan and the Sahara to the south, and Libya to the west. [[Cairo]] is the capital and largest city; Alexandria is the second largest. With over 107 million inhabitants, Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world and the third most populous in Africa. Islam is the official religion and Arabic the official language.

[[Ancient Egypt]], centered on the [[Nile]], traces its heritage to the 6th–4th millennia BC and saw some of the earliest developments of writing, agriculture, urbanization, organized religion, and central government. After nearly three millennia of pharaonic rule, Egypt came under foreign rule in the 6th century BC. It became an early center of Christianity and adopted Islam from the seventh century. Cairo was capital of the Fatimid Caliphate in the tenth century and of the Mamluk Sultanate in the 13th. Egypt became part of the [[Ottoman Empire]] in 1517; its local ruler Muhammad Ali established an autonomous Khedivate in 1867. Occupied by the British, Egypt gained independence in 1922 as a monarchy.

Following the 1952 revolution Egypt became a republic. Under [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]] it nationalized the [[Suez Canal]] after the 1956 crisis. It merged with Syria in 1958 to form the United Arab Republic, which Syria left in 1961. Egypt fought Israel in 1948, 1956, 1967, and 1973, losing the Sinai and the Gaza Strip in 1967; under the 1978 Camp David Accords Israel withdrew from the Sinai, with full control restored in 1982. The 2011 revolution overthrew Hosni Mubarak. Mohamed Morsi, elected in 2012, was removed by the military after mass protests in 2013. The government is a semi-presidential republic led by [[Abdel Fattah el-Sisi]]. Critics cite mass arrests, media censorship, and constitutional amendments extending his rule, and international observers have characterized subsequent elections as neither free nor fair; the government stresses stability and counterterrorism. Egypt has the second-largest economy in Africa.

Source of electric power consisting of one or more electrochemical cells with external connections for powering electrical devices. When a battery supplies power, its positive terminal is the cathode and its negative terminal the anode. Electrons flow from the negative terminal through the external circuit to the positive terminal, driving a [[Redox|redox]] reaction in which higher-energy reactants become lower-energy products and the free-energy difference is delivered as electrical energy. "Battery" once meant a device of multiple cells, but the term now includes single cells.

Primary batteries are used once and discarded, because their electrode materials change irreversibly during discharge; the alkaline battery is a common example. Secondary batteries can be recharged by an applied current that restores the original electrode composition. Examples are the lead–acid automotive battery and the lithium-ion batteries used in portable electronics and electric cars. Sizes range from miniature cells for hearing aids and wristwatches to room-sized banks that provide standby power for telephone exchanges and [[Data center|computer data centers]]. Batteries have much lower specific energy than fuels such as gasoline, a gap partly offset in automobiles by the higher efficiency of electric motors.

[[Benjamin Franklin]] first used the term "battery" in 1749 for linked Leyden jar capacitors. [[Alessandro Volta]] built the first electrochemical battery, the voltaic pile, in 1800: a stack of copper and zinc plates separated by brine-soaked paper disks. Volta did not realize that the voltage came from chemical reactions; [[Michael Faraday]] showed in 1834 that the associated corrosion at the electrodes was unavoidable. The Daniell cell, invented in 1836 by John Frederic Daniell, was the first practical source of electricity and powered telegraph networks. Dry cells, which replaced liquid electrolyte with a paste, made portable devices practical near the end of the 19th century.

Between 2010 and 2018, battery demand grew by 30% annually, reaching 180 GWh in 2018. Production involves mining of lithium, cobalt, and nickel, which can contaminate water sources and ecosystems.

Machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Most electric motors work through the interaction between the motor's magnetic field and current in a wire winding, which generates [[Lorentz force]] as torque on the motor's shaft. An electric generator is mechanically identical but operates inversely, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy.

Motors may be powered by direct current sources such as batteries or rectifiers, or by alternating current sources such as a power grid, inverters, or generators. They may also be classified by construction, application, and type of motion output: brushed or brushless, single-phase, two-phase, or three-phase, axial or radial flux, air-cooled or liquid-cooled. They produce linear or rotary force and are therefore a type of actuator. The largest, used for marine propulsion, pipeline compression, and pumped-storage applications, exceed 100 megawatts. Other uses include fans, blowers, pumps, machine tools, household appliances, power tools, vehicles, disk drives, and electric watches. In regenerative braking, traction motors can be run in reverse as generators to recover energy that would otherwise be lost as heat and friction.

A motor has two mechanical parts: the rotor, which moves, and the stator, which does not. Electrically it consists of field magnets, which may be electromagnets or permanent magnets, and the armature, a set of wire windings on a ferromagnetic core. One is attached to the rotor and the other to the stator, and together they form a magnetic circuit. The stator core is made of thin insulated laminations of electrical steel, which reduce losses from circulating eddy currents. An air gap between stator and rotor allows it to turn and is made as small as possible, since a large gap weakens performance.

In commutated motors, a commutator, a rotary [[Switch|switch]] contacted by carbon brushes, reverses the current in the rotor windings every half turn (180°), so the torque stays in one direction. Such motors have been mostly replaced by brushless designs.

British scientist [[Michael Faraday]] constructed the first primitive electric motor in 1821 using a mercury bath and wire. Moritz Hermann von Jacobi created the first practical rotating motor in 1834, and Thomas Davenport patented a practical direct-current motor in 1837. [[Nikola Tesla]] patented the induction motor in 1888.

Engineering discipline concerned with the study, design, and application of equipment, devices, and systems that use electricity, electronics, and electromagnetism. It emerged as an identifiable occupation in the latter half of the 19th century, after the commercialization of the electric telegraph, the telephone, and electrical power generation, distribution, and use. Electrical engineers typically hold a degree in electrical, electronic, or electrical and electronic engineering, and may belong to professional bodies such as the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) or the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET).

The field encompasses computer engineering, systems engineering, power engineering, telecommunications, radio-frequency engineering, signal processing, instrumentation, control engineering, photovoltaic cells, electronics, and optics and photonics. Many of these overlap with other branches of engineering. Machine learning and computer science were historically developed as fields of electrical engineering. Tools range from a simple voltmeter to sophisticated design and manufacturing software.

William Gilbert drew the first clear distinction between magnetism and static electricity and is credited with establishing the term "electricity." By 1800 [[Alessandro Volta]] had developed the voltaic pile. In 1820 [[Hans Christian Ørsted]] discovered that an electric current produces a magnetic field; William Sturgeon invented the electromagnet in 1825; Georg Ohm quantified the relation between current and potential difference in 1827; [[Michael Faraday]] discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831; Joseph Henry and Edward Davy invented the electrical relay in 1835; and [[James Clerk Maxwell]] published a unified theory of electricity and magnetism in 1873. In 1782 Georges-Louis Le Sage presented in Berlin what was probably the first form of electric telegraphy. Telegraphy may be considered the first example of electrical engineering; by the late 19th century practitioners had built a global telegraph network, and the first professional institutions were founded in the U.K. and the U.S.

An international conference in Chicago in 1893 standardized the units volt, ampere, coulomb, ohm, farad, and henry. Study of electricity was then largely regarded as a subfield of physics; the Technische Universität Darmstadt founded the world's first department of electrical engineering in 1882 and introduced the first degree course in the subject in 1883. [[Thomas Edison]] opened a commercial power plant in lower Manhattan in 1882, serving 59 customers.

Set of physical phenomena associated with the presence and motion of matter possessing an electric charge. Electricity is related to magnetism, both being parts of [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetism]], as described by [[Maxwell's equations]]. Common phenomena include lightning, static electricity, electric heating, and electric discharges.

A positive or negative [[Electric charge|electric charge]] produces an [[Electric field|electric field]]. The motion of charge carriers is an [[Electric current|electric current]] and produces a magnetic field. In most applications, [[Coulomb's law]] determines the force on a charged particle. Electric potential is the work done to move a charge from one position to another within an electric field, typically measured in volts. Electricity serves in electric power, where current energizes equipment, and in electronics, which deals with circuits involving active components such as vacuum tubes, transistors, diodes, and integrated circuits. It is integral to transport, heating and cooling, lighting, communications, and computation.

People were aware of shocks from electric fish long before any knowledge of electricity. Ancient Egyptian texts dating from 2750 BC described them as the "protectors" of all other fish, and writers such as Pliny the Elder and Scribonius Largus attested to the numbing effect of electric catfish and electric rays. Thales of Miletus made observations on static electricity around 600 BC, noting that rubbed amber attracts light objects. In 1600 the English scientist William Gilbert wrote *De Magnete*, distinguishing the lodestone effect from static electricity produced by rubbing amber, and coined the Neo-Latin word *electricus*, from the Greek *elektron*, "amber." The words "electric" and "electricity" first appeared in print in Thomas Browne's *Pseudodoxia Epidemica* of 1646.

[[Benjamin Franklin]] conducted extensive research in the 18th century; in June 1752 he is reputed to have flown a kite in a storm-threatened sky, and sparks jumping from a metal key showed that lightning was electrical. He also explained the Leyden jar in terms of positive and negative charges. In 1791 Luigi Galvani published his discovery that electricity was the medium by which neurons passed signals to muscles. [[Alessandro Volta]]'s voltaic pile of 1800 gave scientists a more reliable source of electrical energy than electrostatic machines. Hans Christian Ørsted and André-Marie Ampère recognized the unity of electric and magnetic phenomena in 1819–1820. [[Michael Faraday]] invented the electric motor in 1821, and Georg Ohm mathematically analyzed the electrical circuit in 1827. James Clerk Maxwell definitively linked electricity, magnetism, and light in 1861 and 1862.

The late 19th century brought the greatest progress in electrical engineering, through figures including Alexander Graham Bell, [[Thomas Edison]], [[Nikola Tesla]], and George Westinghouse, and electricity became an essential tool of modern life; this expansion drove the Second Industrial Revolution. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz found that electrodes illuminated with ultraviolet light create sparks more easily, and in 1905 Albert Einstein explained this photoelectric effect as light energy carried in discrete quantized packets. John Bardeen and Walter Houser Brattain invented the first working transistor, a germanium-based point-contact device, at Bell Labs in 1947.

Self-propagating wave of the [[Electromagnetic field|electromagnetic field]] that carries momentum and radiant energy through space. It is classified by frequency, which is inversely proportional to wavelength, in a spectrum running from radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, to gamma rays. All forms travel at the speed of light in a vacuum and exhibit [[Wave–particle duality|wave–particle duality]], behaving both as waves and as discrete particles called photons.

Electromagnetic radiation is produced by accelerating charged particles and may be emitted naturally, as by the Sun and other celestial bodies, or generated artificially. Its energy needs no propagating medium. Its interaction with matter depends on wavelength, which shapes its uses in communication, medicine, industry, and scientific research. Radio waves enable broadcasting and wireless communication, infrared is used in thermal imaging, and visible light is essential for vision. Higher-energy radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays is applied in medical imaging, cancer treatment, and industrial inspection, and radiation in the ultraviolet and above has been associated with negative health effects.

Electric and magnetic fields obey superposition, so light waves can interfere constructively or destructively. In homogeneous, isotropic media the radiation is a transverse wave: the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, as [[Maxwell's equations]] require. Electromagnetic waves can be polarized, reflected, refracted, or diffracted. In refraction a wave crossing into a medium of different density changes speed and direction, a relation summarized by [[Snell's law]]. Composite light disperses into a visible spectrum when passing through a prism, because the refractive index depends on wavelength.

In quantum mechanics, the radiation consists of photons, uncharged elementary particles with zero rest mass that are the quanta of the electromagnetic field. Wave characteristics are more apparent over large timescales and distances, particle characteristics over small ones; the self-interference of a single photon displays both. Quantum electrodynamics is the theory of how the radiation interacts with matter on an atomic level. Quantum effects provide additional sources, such as the transition of electrons to lower energy levels in an atom and black-body radiation.

Interaction between particles with [[Electric charge|electric charge]], mediated by electromagnetic fields. The electromagnetic force is one of the four fundamental forces of nature and the dominant force in the interactions of atoms and molecules. It describes and relates [[Electricity|electricity]], [[Magnetism|magnetism]], and optics, studied in the subdisciplines of electrostatics, magnetostatics, and electrodynamics. It is the second strongest of the four known fundamental forces and has unlimited range. At high energy it unifies with the weak force as the electroweak interaction.

The electrostatic attraction between atomic nuclei and their electrons holds atoms together, and electric forces allow atoms to combine into molecules; the force is involved in all chemical phenomena. The pushing and pulling forces experienced with ordinary objects result from intermolecular forces. Its technological roles include electrical energy production, transformation, and distribution; light, heat, and sound production and detection; fiber optic and wireless communication; sensors; computation; electrolysis; electroplating; and mechanical motors and actuators.

The phenomenon has been studied since ancient times to explain lightning and static electricity and the attraction between magnetized pieces of iron ore and compasses. In the 18th and 19th centuries scientists developed mathematical relationships between these phenomena and electric charges and currents. They showed that electrical and magnetic phenomena were related and could create self-sustaining electromagnetic waves, which form visible light and other [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]], including gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves, and radio waves.

Mathematically, electromagnetism is described by electromagnetic fields, quantities that give the electric and magnetic influence at a given location and time. A disturbance in the electric field can create a disturbance in the magnetic field, which in turn affects the electric field, producing an oscillation that propagates through space as an electromagnetic wave. Six quantities describe the fields in three distinct cases: the electric field E and magnetic flux density B; the displacement field D and magnetic field strength H for charges responding within a material; and the electric potential V and magnetic vector potential A. [[Maxwell's equations]] encapsulate the relations among these fields.

The theory's requirement that observations stay consistent across moving frames of reference, and the fixing of the speed of light by the permeability and permittivity of the medium, helped inspire Einstein's theory of special relativity in 1905. Quantum electrodynamics modifies Maxwell's equations to be consistent with the quantized nature of matter, expressing changes in the field as discrete excitations called photons, the quanta of light.

[[Subatomic particle]] whose electric charge is negative one elementary charge. It is an elementary particle contained in the matter that makes up the universe. Its charge is −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs and its rest mass approximately 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, about ⁠1/1836⁠ that of a proton. All atoms are composed of electrons together with protons and neutrons, and in atoms an electron's matter wave occupies [[Atomic orbital|atomic orbitals]] around the positively charged nucleus. The configuration and energy levels of an atom's electrons determine its chemical properties. The outermost, or valence, electrons are the least tightly bound and form chemical bonds between atoms to create molecules and crystals.

Electrons belong to the first generation of the [[Lepton|lepton]] family, elementary particles that do not interact with the strong nuclear force. They have no known substructure. Their intrinsic angular momentum (spin) is half the reduced Planck constant, ħ/2. As fermions, no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state, according to the [[Pauli exclusion principle]]. Electrons show properties of both particles and waves, and can be diffracted like light. They are subject to gravity, electromagnetism, and the weak interaction. A moving electron generates a magnetic field, and it radiates or absorbs energy as photons when accelerated. Its antiparticle, the [[Positron|positron]], is identical except for opposite charge; when the two collide they can annihilate, producing gamma ray photons. Electrons can be created in [[Beta decay|beta decay]] of radioactive isotopes and in high-energy collisions, as when cosmic rays enter the atmosphere.

The concept explains many phenomena. In metals the outermost electrons are delocalized and move freely, accounting for high electrical and thermal conductivity. In semiconductors the number of mobile charge carriers, electrons and holes, can be tuned by doping, temperature, voltage, and radiation, which is the basis of modern electronics. Free electron beams in a vacuum are used in cathode ray tubes, electron microscopes, electron beam welding, lithography, and particle accelerators.

The ancient Greeks noticed that amber attracted small objects when rubbed with fur. In his 1600 treatise *De Magnete*, William Gilbert coined the Neo-Latin term *electrica* for such substances, from the Greek *ēlektron*, "amber." The English physicist J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 through experiments with cathode rays, showing that they consist of negatively charged particles much smaller than atoms. [[Robert Millikan]] measured its charge in 1909.

Scientific and engineering discipline that applies the principles of physics to design, create, and operate devices that manipulate electrons and other electrically charged particles. A subfield of physics and [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineering]], it uses active devices such as [[Transistor|transistors]], diodes, and [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] to control and amplify the flow of electric current and to convert it from one form to another, such as alternating current to direct current or analog signals to digital signals. Electronic devices have influenced telecommunications, entertainment, education, health care, industry, and security. The semiconductor industry is the main driving force behind the advance of electronics and is one of the global economy's largest and most profitable industries, with annual revenues exceeding $481 billion in 2018.

Karl Ferdinand Braun's crystal detector in 1874, the first semiconductor device, and the identification of the electron in 1897 by Joseph John Thomson, followed by the invention of the vacuum tube, inaugurated the field. Ambrose Fleming's diode and [[Lee de Forest]]'s triode of the early 1900s made small voltages, such as radio signals from an antenna, detectable. Vacuum tubes, the first active components, enabled radio, television, radar, and long-distance telephony; by the 1920s commercial radio broadcasting was widespread. [[John Bardeen]] and Walter Houser Brattain invented the first working point-contact transistor at [[Bell Labs]] in 1947. Vacuum tubes remained important in microwave and high-power transmission and in television receivers until the middle of the 1980s, and are still used in specialist applications such as guitar amplifiers.

In April 1955 the IBM 608, containing more than 3,000 germanium transistors, became the first all-transistorized calculator manufactured for the commercial market, and IBM ordered all future products to use transistors. The MOSFET, invented at Bell Labs between 1955 and 1960, was the first truly compact transistor that could be miniaturized and mass-produced, and it revolutionized the industry. The integrated circuit of [[Jack Kilby]] and Robert Noyce placed all components on one block of semiconductor material, leading to small-scale integration in the early 1960s and medium-scale integration in the late 1960s. In 2008 billion-transistor processors became commercially available.

Components are active, such as transistors and thyristors, or passive: capacitors, inductors, and resistors. They are usually soldered to a [[Printed circuit board|printed circuit board]]. Circuits are divided into analog, which use a continuous range of voltage or current, and digital, which use discrete levels.

Queen of England and Ireland (r. 1558–1603), the last and longest-reigning monarch of the [[House of Tudor]]. Her reign gave its name to the Elizabethan era.

Elizabeth was the only surviving child of [[Henry VIII]] and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. When she was two years old her parents' marriage was annulled, her mother was executed, and she was declared illegitimate; Henry restored her to the line of succession when she was 10. After Henry's death in 1547, her half-brother [[Edward VI]] ruled until 1553, bequeathing the crown to Lady Jane Grey, but his will was set aside and the Catholic [[Mary I|Mary]] became queen. During Mary's reign Elizabeth was imprisoned for nearly a year on suspicion of supporting Protestant rebels.

On Mary's death in 1558 Elizabeth succeeded and set out to rule by good counsel, relying heavily on advisers led by William Cecil, whom she created Baron Burghley. One of her first actions was establishing an English church, of which she became supreme governor; this Elizabethan Religious Settlement would evolve into the [[Church of England]]. She never married despite numerous courtships, and was therefore sometimes called the "Virgin Queen." She was succeeded by her first cousin twice removed, James VI of Scotland.

Elizabeth was more moderate in government than her father and siblings, and relatively tolerant in religion. After the pope declared her illegitimate in 1570, which in theory released English Catholics from allegiance to her, several conspiracies threatened her life; all were defeated with the help of the secret service run by Francis Walsingham. She was cautious in foreign affairs, maneuvering between France and Spain, and half-heartedly supported several poorly resourced military campaigns in the Netherlands, France, and Ireland. By the mid-1580s England could no longer avoid war with Spain.

A cult of personality grew around her, celebrated in portraits, pageants, and literature. The Elizabethan era is known for the flourishing of English drama, led by [[William Shakespeare]] and [[Christopher Marlowe]], for maritime adventurers such as [[Francis Drake]], and for the defeat of the Spanish Armada. Some historians depict her as short-tempered and sometimes indecisive, and economic and military problems weakened her popularity late in her reign. Her 44 years on the throne provided stability after the short reigns of her half-siblings and helped forge a sense of national identity.
